strengths: Rigorous theoretical analysis proving that nested submodel learning recovers the Pareto front while post-training selection and all-submodel learning fail (Theorems 4.1-4.3 for linear models)
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across diverse architectures (LLaMA 1B/3B/8B, ViT-L/H/7B, GPT-2) showing consistent improvements in graceful degradation
Figure 3 demonstrates FLEXRANK recovers true Pareto front on toy models, validating core theoretical insight
Well-motivated practical problem with clear 'train-once, deploy-everywhere' paradigm
Detailed implementation for multiple layer types (linear, convolutional, attention) with explicit hyperparameters
weaknesses: Severe training limitation: only 10,000 steps (~0.5 epoch) due to computational constraints, with authors acknowledging 'expected improvements with additional compute' but providing no concrete evidence of convergence or final performance

Dynamic programming validity unclear: DP is exact only under additivity assumption (which is violated); no comparison of DP-selected configurations to oracle optimal ones
Missing comparisons with FlexTron (Cai et al., 2024) and LlamaFlex (Cai et al., 2025), the most recent elastic model training methods, despite addressing the same problem

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem of deploying models across heterogeneous hardware with different computational budgets

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple architectures (GPT-2, Llama, ViT models) showing consistent improvements over SVD baselines
Well-structured three-stage pipeline with clear motivation for each component
Thorough ablation studies demonstrating the necessity of joint submodel training and showing advantages over independent per-model optimization
weaknesses: Critical theory-practice gap: theoretical results (Section 4) apply only to linear models; extension to non-linear networks lacks rigor and formal justification

Severely limited experimental validation: only 10,000 training steps (~half an epoch) due to computational constraints; no convergence plots showing stabilization; unclear if results have converged
Missing statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests across experiments; improvements over DataSVD+DP often appear marginal
Incomplete baseline comparisons: no experimental comparison with FLEXTRON or LLAMAFLEX despite positioning them as related work; excuse of unavailable code is inadequate

Pareto front validation (Fig. 3) only demonstrated on 4-layer network with MNIST; extrapolation to thousand-layer models like Llama-8B is unjustified
Missing critical experiments: no convergence analysis, no sensitivity to hyperparameter K, no wall-clock latency measurements on real hardware, no actual downstream task training with full epochs

strengths: Rigorous theoretical analysis: Theorems 4.1-4.3 formally characterize why existing approaches fail and prove nested learning recovers the Pareto front, providing genuine insight into weight-sharing interference

Principled methodology with strong empirical validation: Each component (DataSVD, DP, nestedness, distillation) is well-motivated; comprehensive experiments across diverse models (LLMs up to 8B, ViTs) with consistent improvements
Clear problem motivation and solution: Articulates gaps in existing PEFT and compression methods; proposes elegant nested structure solution that addresses representation sharing problem
Strong practical results with graceful degradation: Maintains ~5% accuracy margin at 30% parameters for ViTs; shows consistent improvements over baselines across different model families and scales
Thorough ablation studies: Figures 6-8 effectively validate importance of each component (parameter importance, distillation necessity, joint training requirement)
Computational efficiency of DP search: O(L·K) solution vs. O(K^L) brute force is practical; layer-wise probing strategy is sensible
weaknesses: Theory-practice gap: Theoretical analysis restricted to linear models (Section 4) while applied to deep non-linear networks; critical assumption that importance ordering is preserved validated only on small 4-layer MNIST network (Fig. 3), not realistic scales

Strong unvalidated assumptions in DP phase: Additivity of approximation errors across layers acknowledged as strong but essential; for networks with complex information flow (esp. Transformers), validity unclear; no analysis of DP approximation error on actual networks

Substantial computational training cost: Requires 2-8 A100-64GB nodes for 2-6 days even with limited 10K steps; limits practical adoption despite being better than training from scratch; authors acknowledge room for improvement but don't address it

Limited baseline comparisons: Missing experimental comparisons with recent elastic methods FLEXTRON and LLAMAFLEX despite being relevant; comparisons primarily against SVD-based and ACIP methods; Table 2 mostly qualitative

Incomplete practical efficiency analysis: No actual inference latency/throughput measurements despite claiming computational gains; Section 3.5 is theoretical; hardware-specific efficiency analysis absent, limiting deployment utility assessment

Insufficient downstream task validation: NLP evaluation on proxy dataset and zero-shot commonsense tasks, not pretraining distribution; ViT only on ImageNet-1K; post-adaptation shows severe degradation for smallest models (Table 1: code accuracy drops from 36.78% to 1.22%)

DP search validation gaps: Layer-wise sensitivity matrix S evaluated independently despite additivity assumption; no sensitivity analysis for DP parameters or robustness to errors in S; toy problem (Fig. 3) insufficient for realistic scale validation

Generalizability concerns: Method specifically for weight matrix factorization; extension to architectural elasticity and other model types unclear; coverage of non-linear components (norm layers, residuals) not fully specified

strengths: Rigorous theoretical analysis proving why nested submodel training recovers Pareto fronts (Theorems 4.1-4.3), with clear insights on representational interference in competing objectives
Comprehensive experimental validation across diverse architectures (CNNs, ViTs, LLMs) and tasks (NLP, CV) with extensive ablations and controlled experiments validating core claims
Practical system design with DataSVD initialization, efficient O(L·K) DP algorithm, and GAR reparametrization that translates theoretical savings to measured speedups (Figure 10)
Consistently strong empirical results showing graceful performance degradation (70% compression with <5% drop on ViTs) and competitive with or outperforming multiple baselines
Honest treatment of limitations, detailed reproducibility information with promised code release, and thorough appendices with implementation details and hyperparameters
weaknesses: Critical theory-practice gap: theoretical results (Section 4) proved only for linear models; core DP assumption (additive errors across layers) validated empirically only on MNIST (4-layer network), not on actual LLMs or large ViTs where nonlinearity may violate assumptions

Ranking-preservation assumption (page 3) asserted rather than proven for deep nonlinear networks; no analysis of when this assumption breaks down or sensitivity to violations; insufficient justification for why this holds in complex networks with nonlinear dependencies

Limited technical novelty: DataSVD acknowledged as not new, distillation and low-rank decomposition are standard, GAR explicitly stated as not exclusive to FlexRank; primary novelty is combination rather than fundamental innovation

Incomplete experimental design: sensitivity to calibration data size/diversity not studied, LoRA finetuning shows severe degradation at 0.4× compression on code tasks (Table 1), vision experiments only on ImageNet1K, no validation of DP assumptions on large realistic networks

Non-trivial training overhead (2× memory, 2× slowdown, requires teacher-student) and inference speedups dependent on specific hardware/kernel implementations; practical adoption concerns for large-scale deployment

Honest discussion of limitations including training efficiency costs (2× overhead) and theory-practice gap
